title: Serbia's budget bailouts keep Resavica underground coal mines running
programme: State budget support to JP PEU Resavica underground coal mines
problem: Serbia's state-owned underground coal mines (JP PEU Resavica), which supply part of EPS's coal, cannot cover their own costs.
solution: The government made direct budget transfers, gave an interest-free conditional loan and reprogrammed or tolerated unpaid taxes, while state utility EPS lent to the mines and tolerated their unpaid electricity bills.
implementer: Government of Serbia and Tax Administration
funding: State budget transfers, foregone tax revenue and loans from the budget, the Development Fund and EPS.
results: The budget subsidy to Resavica almost doubled in 2021, driving a 42% rise in Serbia's direct coal subsidies; Serbia was the region's largest coal subsidiser, at EUR 98.67 million over 2021-2022.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own case: budget money and EPS support prop up loss-making coal mining. The Energy Community Secretariat tracks these subsidies against the Western Balkan commitment to phase out coal subsidies and respect State aid rules.
adapt_needed: Replace open-ended bailouts with a time-bound mine closure and worker transition plan, with any remaining aid assessed under State aid rules.
blockers: Mining jobs in coal towns and EPS's reliance on domestic coal make cutting support politically difficult.
quote: In Serbia, main driver for increase of 42% is almost doubled subsidy from the state budget to JP PEU Resavica of RSD 8,5 billion (EUR 36 million) in 2021.

title: Serbia's state guarantees on EPS coal loans build growing fiscal exposure
programme: State loan guarantees for EPS coal plant and mine investments
problem: EPS needed large loans for desulphurisation, mine equipment, a new 350 MW unit at Kostolac B and refinancing of its debts.
solution: The Ministry of Finance guaranteed EPS loans from JICA, China Exim Bank, EBRD, KfW and the World Bank (IBRD), giving the utility cheaper credit than comparable commercial loans.
funding: Loans from development banks and export-credit lenders, guaranteed by the state.
results: The subsidy value of this public finance support rose from EUR 12.02 million in 2021 to EUR 22.98 million in 2022; Serbia's outstanding state-backed coal support (guarantees, budget loans and arrears) reached EUR 701.9 million, 7.1% of general government expenditure.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own case: the state backs EPS's lignite investments with guarantees, including on EBRD, KfW and World Bank loans. The Energy Community Secretariat counts these guarantees as coal subsidies that Serbia has committed to phase out.
adapt_needed: Redirect state guarantees and development-bank lending from extending coal units towards grids, storage and renewables.
blockers: Guarantees already issued run for up to 20 years, so the fiscal exposure cannot be unwound quickly.
quote: Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia are the Contracting Parties where the level of direct subsidies increased in 2021 compared to 2020. The increase is primarily the result from issuing additional state guarantees for loans to thermal power plants and continuing the policy of tolerating the non-payment by coal mines as well as support to production of coal.

title: Bosnia's guarantees and tolerated arrears sustain loss-making coal mines and plants
programme: FBiH state guarantee for Tuzla block 7 and tolerated coal-mine arrears
problem: State-owned coal mines in the Federation of BiH run up large unpaid taxes, contributions and concession fees, and state utility EPBiH sought finance for new coal capacity.
solution: Governments tolerated and reprogrammed the mines' arrears, the FBiH Government guaranteed a China Exim Bank loan for the new Tuzla block 7, and EPBiH invested in, lent to and prepaid its supplying mines.
implementer: Government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina
funding: Foregone public revenue, state loan guarantees and loans and capital injections from the state-owned utility.
results: Direct subsidies were EUR 36.04 million in 2021 and EUR 34.1 million in 2022, the highest per MWh in the region at EUR 3.09/MWh in 2021; outstanding state-backed support reached EUR 1,022.8 million, 23.1% of general government expenditure.
serbia_reason: Like Serbia, BiH supports lignite mines and plants through state-owned utilities, guarantees and tolerated arrears. It shows how these hidden supports pile up contingent liabilities that conflict with the Energy Community commitment to phase out coal subsidies.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to audit EPS advances to mines and tolerated debts and report them transparently as State aid.
blockers: The social role of coal mines and close utility-mine ties make arrears politically hard to collect.
quote: Main driver for increased subsidies in Bosnia and Herzegovina is continuing the policy of tolerating the non-payment of due debts and arrears, SOE investments in coal mines as well as changing difference between the underlying interest rates used for valuation of subsidies in the form of State guarantees.

title: Montenegro winds down direct subsidies to Pljevlja coal mine and plant
programme: Repayment of rescheduled Pljevlja coal mine tax debt
problem: The Pljevlja coal mine, owned by majority state-owned utility EPCG, had accumulated tax and contribution arrears.
solution: The government rescheduled the arrears over five years, the mine repaid them early in January 2021, and no new fiscal or SOE investment support followed; only a state guarantee on a KfW loan for filter replacement at TPP Pljevlja remained.
implementer: Government of Montenegro (Ministry of Finance, Tax Administration)
funding: The mine repaid its rescheduled debt; filter replacement was financed by a state-guaranteed KfW loan.
results: Direct coal subsidies fell every year from EUR 0.73 million in 2018 to EUR 0.06 million in 2022, their lowest level in the period.
serbia_reason: Montenegro's only lignite plant is run by a majority state-owned utility, as EPS's plants are. Clearing tax arrears and ending new support shows a Contracting Party can meet the Energy Community subsidy phase-out commitment, using a KfW loan only for pollution control.
adapt_needed: Serbia's much larger mining sector would need a phased schedule for settling mine arrears rather than a single repayment.
blockers: Serbia's loss-making underground mines could not repay their arrears without restructuring or closure.
quote: In Montenegro, tax debt reprogrammed in 2021 was paid out and no new fiscal support occurred in 2022 as well as SOE investments. Still some support was provided in the form of Public finance support as state loan guarantee for filters replacement in the TPP Pljevlja.

title: North Macedonia adds no new coal subsidies, but ageing plants falter
programme: State loan guarantees for TPP Bitola modernisation
problem: North Macedonia's state utility ESM relies on ageing lignite plants at Bitola and Oslomej while domestic coal quality and supply decline.
solution: The government gave no new direct subsidies in 2021-2022, limiting support to two existing state guarantees on commercial loans for modernising TPP Bitola.
implementer: Ministry of Finance of North Macedonia
funding: Commercial bank loans of EUR 49 million and EUR 30 million, guaranteed by the state.
results: Subsidies per MWh of coal power fell from EUR 0.81 in 2018 to EUR 0.06 in 2022 and totalled EUR 0.57 million in 2021-2022, but REK Bitola suffered numerous breakdowns and Oslomej ran on imported coal.
serbia_reason: Like Serbia, North Macedonia's coal power is run by a vertically integrated state utility. It shows that cutting subsidies, as the Energy Community commitment requires, does not by itself fix ageing plants or falling coal supply.
adapt_needed: Pair subsidy cuts with a dated plan to replace old lignite units so the utility does not drift into costly coal imports.
blockers: Coal still provides most of Serbia's electricity, so ending support quickly would risk supply shortfalls.
quote: There were no new direct subsidies for electricity generation from coal in 2021-2022, except for the existing public finance support in the form of two state loan guarantees for the modernization of TPP Bitola (see Annex 4).

title: Kosovo's budget loans cover KEK operating losses from inefficient lignite plants
programme: Government loans to KEK and guarantee for the World Bank Energy Clean-up and Land Reclamation loan
problem: Kosovo's state-owned KEK runs old lignite plants with low efficiency and poor bill collection, so it cannot cover its operating costs.
solution: The Ministry of Finance lent KEK budget money at below-market interest to cover regular operations and guaranteed a World Bank (IDA) loan for energy clean-up and land reclamation.
funding: Government budget loans and a state-guaranteed World Bank IDA loan.
results: Subsidies were EUR 4.89 million in 2021 and EUR 5.65 million in 2022, below 2016-2017 levels because no new measures were added; the 2022 rise came from an extra loan to meet KEK's public service obligation.
serbia_reason: KEK, like EPS, is a vertically integrated state utility whose lignite plants and mines need state help. It shows how operating losses turn into recurring state loans that the Energy Community counts as coal subsidies.
adapt_needed: Tie any state support to EPS to efficiency and bill-collection targets and a closure timeline for the oldest units.
blockers: Keeping end-user prices low is a political priority, so utility losses and state support are likely to persist.
quote: The fiscal support subsidies for electricity generation from coal in Kosovo* were related to the government loan to cover the cost of KEK's regular operating activities caused by the low operational efficiency of the TPP and problems with the collection of electricity bills, in the amount the EUR 4,79 million and EUR 5,53 million in 2021 and 2022 respectively (see Annex 2).
